profile.reading: This is a Barclays owned and directly operated data center in or near Union, Union County, New Jersey, tracked by a specialized data center site impact monitor that rates it small in scale relative to major colocation or hyperscale facilities in the broader Newark and New York City tristate market, though that source gives no specific megawatt or square footage figure. No confirmed year built was found in sourcing checked this session. This registrys coordinate check found a second, separate Barclays operator entry elsewhere in this registry tagged to Middlesex County, New Jersey, roughly 13 kilometers away, which this registry treats as a genuinely distinct second New Jersey facility rather than a duplicate of this Union County site, since the two carry clearly different coordinates rather than matching exactly. Barclays is a major British multinational bank with substantial United States investment banking and technology operations, and maintains data center infrastructure in both the United States and its home market in the United Kingdom, including a roughly 10 megawatt facility on Rowdell Road in Northolt, Middlesex, England, for context on the companys broader data center footprint beyond this New Jersey site. Barclays traces its origins to 1690, when two Quakers established a London goldsmith banking business, with the modern joint stock company formed in 1896 through the merger of twelve banks across London and the English provinces; the bank is today headquartered at One Churchill Place in Londons Canary Wharf district, employing roughly 100,000 people across more than 40 countries and reporting about 29.1 billion pounds in 2025 revenue. Barclays significantly expanded its United States footprint in 2008 by acquiring the North American operations of the collapsed Lehman Brothers, gaining a substantial presence in US equities and investment banking that helps explain the banks continued need for New Jersey area data center infrastructure supporting its American trading and technology operations.
profile.acquisition: Acquired by Barclays Capital on 22 September 2008 as part of its purchase of Lehman Brothers North American investment banking and capital markets business. The bankruptcy court set the real estate consideration at 1.29 billion dollars, of which 330 million dollars was for the two New Jersey data centers, Cranford and Piscataway, together; the split between the two sites was not disclosed.
profile.capacity_note: No IT capacity, floor area or power figure for this site has been published by Lehman Brothers, Barclays, or the bankruptcy court record. Private corporate facilities of this kind publish no spec sheet.
profile.facility_type: private enterprise data center, financial services
profile.research_note: Fresh research via More Than Just Parks data center tracker and DC Hub, both showing this Union County, NJ coordinate. Corrected a suggestion from initial research that this row and the separate Middlesex County Barclays row might be duplicates of one building, since this registrys own coordinate data for the two rows shows a roughly 13 kilometer separation, indicating genuinely distinct facilities rather than a duplicate tag.

reading.body:
No information on the power consumption, floor area, or IT capacity of this facility has been published by Lehman Brothers, Barclays, or the bankruptcy court record that transferred it in 2008. The site cannot be ranked among AI infrastructure by capacity.

Barclays acquired this Cranford facility as part of its purchase of Lehman Brothers' North American operations in September 2008, paying a combined $330 million for two New Jersey data centers without public disclosure of how that valuation split between them. The facility operated as a Lehman Brothers private enterprise data center for financial services before the acquisition and remains a private corporate facility that publishes no spec sheet.

New Jersey has 48 mapped data center facilities and 5 with published power figures totaling 111.3 MW. This facility's position in that ranking cannot be determined because no capacity figure exists in the public record. It holds significance only as a historical asset acquired during the 2008 financial crisis and as part of Barclays' private infrastructure portfolio, not as a known contributor to the state's measurable AI-supporting compute capacity.
